chapters.name: A sealed machine
chapters.note: great for using models, useless for opening them

cap.1: Open-source tools were great for using and training models, and had almost nothing for opening one up and watching it think. So Neel Nanda wrote one.
cap.2: After leaving Anthropic's interpretability team, Neel Nanda found tooling for using and training models but little for digging inside. TransformerLens filled the gap.
cap.3: TransformerLens (Nanda, 2022), heavily inspired by Anthropic's internal Garcon, aims for the shortest loop from experiment idea to result. It loads 15,000+ models across 140+ architecture families.

cap.1: Picture the model as a glass-walled factory with a labelled tap on every belt. Run it once and a jar at every tap fills up, all lined up on one shelf.
cap.2: A HookedTransformer is a normal transformer with a named HookPoint at every activation. run_with_cache runs it once and hands back every activation by name.
cap.3: Every intermediate tensor passes a HookPoint with a stable name. The naming scheme is shared across architectures, so an experiment written for GPT-2 small transfers.

cap.1: One run fills every jar. Then you lift jars off the shelf by a short label: which kind of value, and which layer.
cap.2: logits, cache = model.run_with_cache(tokens), then cache['pattern', 0] is layer 0's attention pattern. The shorthand expands to blocks.0.attn.hook_pattern.
cap.3: run_with_cache returns an ActivationCache keyed by hook name; utils.get_act_name('pattern', 0) gives 'blocks.0.attn.hook_pattern'. Pass remove_batch_dim=True for one sequence.

chapters.name: Tidied before delivery
chapters.verdict: Same predictions, different parameters. Pick one mode per notebook.

cap.1: The factory tidies its machines before handing them over. What comes out is identical, but the parts inside no longer match the original blueprints.
cap.2: from_pretrained folds LayerNorm into the next linear layer and centres some weights by default. Predictions are unchanged, parameters are not, so ln1.w prints as all ones.
cap.3: fold_ln absorbs LayerNorm's scale and bias into W_Q/W_K/W_V, W_in or W_U; centring removes directions invisible after LayerNorm or softmax. Disable all three to check a reimplementation.

cap.1: Every tap works both ways: read what flows past, or swap in something else and watch what changes downstream. Reading comes first; changing comes next.
cap.2: The cache is for reading. Hooks, the next node, let a function edit an activation mid-run, which is how you test whether a part actually causes a behaviour.
cap.3: Hook points support caching, editing, ablating or replacing any activation during the forward pass: the substrate for every patching and ablation experiment that follows.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Print ln1.w early: which mode did you load?
Too big to fit? nnsight, same idea remotely

cap.1: This is the instrument for the rest of the course. Every look inside a model in chapter 1 starts with loading it here and running it once.
cap.2: Loading gpt2-small, caching and hooking is the setup step from [1.2] to [1.5]. For models too big for your machine, nnsight does the same job over a remote backend.
cap.3: Understanding and steering a model starts with reliable access to its internals under stable names, and knowing what preprocessing did to the weights keeps conclusions about the real model.

hamming.what: A library that loads real models with a named tap on every internal activation, so you can read or change them during a forward pass.
hamming.when: At the start of every interpretability experiment in chapter 1, whenever the model fits on your machine.
hamming.why: Stable names and one-line caching keep the loop from idea to result short, which is what makes exploratory interpretability feasible.
